name: Tibialis anterior
func: The muscle along the front of the shin. It lifts the foot and toes up (dorsiflexion), stops the foot slapping down when you walk, and helps turn the sole inward.

levels.kid:
Put your finger just to the outside of your shinbone and lift your toes up toward your nose. Feel a muscle get hard? That is the **tibialis anterior**.

Its job is to **lift the front of your foot up**. That keeps your toes from dragging on the ground when you swing your leg forward to walk.

It also lets your foot come down **gently** after your heel touches the ground, instead of going "slap!" If this muscle stops working, people can trip over their own toes.
levels.hs:
The **tibialis anterior** is the largest muscle of the **anterior compartment** of the leg. It lies just under the skin, right beside the **lateral (outer) surface of the tibia**, so you can feel it along the front of the shin.

It starts from the **lateral condyle** and upper half of the lateral surface of the tibia and from the **interosseous membrane**. Its fleshy belly becomes a thick tendon in the lower third of the leg. This tendon passes in front of the ankle, under the **extensor retinacula** (bands that hold tendons in place), and inserts on the **medial cuneiform** and the base of the **first metatarsal**, on the inner side of the foot.

Actions: it is the strongest **dorsiflexor** of the ankle (pulling the foot up), and it **inverts** the foot (turns the sole inward). During walking, it lifts the toes to clear the ground in swing and lowers the foot smoothly after heel strike. It also helps support the **medial arch**.

It is supplied by the **deep fibular (peroneal) nerve** (L4–L5). Next to it, laterally, lie the **extensor hallucis longus** and **extensor digitorum longus**, and the **anterior tibial artery** runs deep to it on the interosseous membrane.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** origin from the lateral condyle and upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia, the interosseous membrane and the deep fascia. Insertion: the medial and inferior surfaces of the **medial cuneiform** and the base of the **first metatarsal**. With **fibularis longus**, which inserts on the same two bones from below, it forms a "**stirrup**" under the midfoot.

**Anterior compartment contents:** tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius, plus the **anterior tibial artery** and **deep fibular nerve**. At the ankle, from medial to lateral, the order is: **tibialis anterior tendon, extensor hallucis longus, anterior tibial artery (becoming dorsalis pedis), deep fibular nerve, extensor digitorum longus** ("Tom Has A Very Nice Dog": tendon, hallucis, artery, vein, nerve, digitorum). The compartment is enclosed by the tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and tough deep fascia, so it cannot expand.

**Innervation:** the **deep fibular nerve** (L4–L5, mainly L4 for tibialis anterior), a branch of the common fibular nerve. **Blood supply:** the anterior tibial artery.

**Gait:** activity peaks just after **heel strike**, when it contracts eccentrically to lower the forefoot (controlling plantarflexion), and during **swing**, when it lifts the foot to clear the ground. It is also active in standing when balance shifts backward.

**Tendon sheath:** a synovial sheath surrounds the tendon from above the superior extensor retinaculum to near its insertion, which can become inflamed in overuse.
levels.phd:
The tibialis anterior is a key muscle in the **neural control of locomotion**. Its alternation with the soleus during walking is a classic example of **reciprocal flexor–extensor patterns** produced partly by spinal **central pattern generators** and modulated by descending input. In humans, transcranial magnetic stimulation shows tibialis anterior receives strong **corticospinal** input during the swing phase, more than the calf muscles, which is why it is especially affected after strokes and spinal cord injuries; this cortical dependence makes it a common target in rehabilitation research.

Its fibre composition is relatively high in **type I** fibres (around 70% in many samples), which fits its sustained activity in gait and balance. However, it can produce rapid force during quick dorsiflexion, and it is a standard muscle for studying **rate of force development** and motor unit discharge rates with high-density surface EMG.

Tibialis anterior is often used to study **motor unit remodelling with ageing**: elderly people have fewer, larger motor units in this muscle as surviving axons reinnervate denervated fibres.

Clinically oriented research has used **functional electrical stimulation (FES)** of the common fibular nerve to drive tibialis anterior during swing in people with foot drop. Devices triggered by a heel switch or motion sensors can restore toe clearance and may produce lasting improvements in voluntary control, possibly through spinal and cortical plasticity, though the size of this carryover effect varies across trials.

Its tendon is relatively thick and is studied for **tendon degeneration**, typically at its insertion in older adults.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** ask the patient to walk on their heels (tests dorsiflexion) and resist dorsiflexion and inversion. Weakness causes **foot drop**: a **steppage (high-stepping) gait** to lift the toes clear, and a **foot slap** after heel strike.

**Localising foot drop:**
**Common fibular nerve palsy** at the fibular neck (most common): weak dorsiflexion and **eversion**, but **inversion preserved** (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve). Numbness on the dorsum of the foot.
**L5 radiculopathy**: weak dorsiflexion and **inversion** (tibialis posterior is also L5), hip abduction weakness, back pain radiating to the dorsum of the foot.
**Sciatic nerve injury**: also weak hamstrings and calf.
**Other causes**: stroke (with upper motor neuron signs), motor neurone disease, and **Charcot–Marie–Tooth** disease (an inherited neuropathy with distal wasting and high-arched feet). EMG and nerve conduction studies distinguish these.

**Anterior compartment syndrome** may follow tibial fracture or crush injury; pain on passive plantarflexion of the toes and numbness of the **first web space** (deep fibular nerve) are early clues. **Chronic exertional compartment syndrome** causes predictable shin pain during running that eases with rest; it is confirmed by compartment pressure testing.

**Tibialis anterior tendon rupture** is rare, usually in older adults, with a painless or minimally painful foot drop and a lump in front of the ankle. **Shin splints** (medial tibial stress syndrome) mainly involve the posteromedial tibia, but anterior shin pain in runners can involve this muscle.

Management of foot drop includes an **ankle–foot orthosis (AFO)**, physiotherapy, FES, and in permanent cases **tendon transfer** of tibialis posterior to the dorsum of the foot.

keyPoints: Muscle along the lateral side of the shin, anterior compartment
Inserts on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base
Main dorsiflexor; also inverts the foot
Weakness → foot drop with steppage gait and foot slap

test.q: What is the main action of tibialis anterior?
test.explain: It is the strongest muscle lifting the foot up.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the tibialis anterior? (three words)
test.explain: The deep fibular nerve supplies all the anterior compartment muscles.

test.q: In common fibular nerve palsy, which movement is preserved?
test.explain: Inversion by tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) is spared, unlike in L5 radiculopathy.

test.q: Weakness of tibialis anterior produces what gait?
test.explain: Patients lift the knee high to clear the dropped foot.

test.q: Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial ______ and the first metatarsal.
test.explain: With fibularis longus inserting nearby, it forms a stirrup under the midfoot.
